steps.observation: Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
Here are the key differences between DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) and RNA (ribonucleic acid):

1. Sugar component  
   • DNA contains deoxyribose (one less oxygen on the 2′ carbon)  
   • RNA contains ribose (has a hydroxyl group on the 2′ carbon)

2. Nitrogenous bases  
   • DNA uses adenine (A), cytosine (C), guanine (G) and thymine (T)  
   • RNA uses adenine (A), cytosine (C), guanine (G) and uracil (U) (replaces thymine)

3. Strandedness  
   • DNA is typically double-stranded (the famous double helix)  
   • RNA is usually single-stranded, though it can fold back on itself to form secondary structures

4. Function  
   • DNA stores and transmits genetic information from one generation to the next  
   • RNA plays several roles in decoding that information and making proteins—mRNA (messenger), tRNA (transfer), rRNA (ribosomal) plus regulatory RNAs

5. Location in the cell  
   • In eukaryotes, DNA is mainly in the nucleus (and in mitochondria/chloroplasts)  
   • RNA is synthesized in the nucleus but functions mostly in the cytoplasm

6. Stability  
   • DNA is chemically more stable (de-oxy sugar and double helix protect it)  
   • RNA is more prone to hydrolysis (the extra OH on ribose and single strand make it less stable)

7. Length and abundance  
   • DNA molecules are very long (millions of bases), one or a few per cell  
   • RNA molecules are shorter (hundreds to thousands of bases) and many types coexist in the same cell

Summary: DNA is the long-term, stable repository of genetic information made of deoxyribose and thymine in a double helix. RNA is a shorter, more versatile molecule with ribose and uracil, generally single-stranded, that carries out the work of interpreting and using the DNA code.
